title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show
desc:
These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?

Who knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?

To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.

title: Meta Ordered To Pay New Mexico $25 Billion Over Misleading Privacy Claims
desc:
Meta Ordered To Pay New Mexico $25 Billion Over Misleading Privacy Claims

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

A Santa Fe judge on Wednesday ordered Meta Platforms to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company committed 43.9 million violations of state consumer-protection law by making misleading statements about Facebook users' data privacy and control.

The case, filed in 2021, grew out of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. New Mexico alleged that Facebook, now Meta, systematically misled the public - and New Mexico users - about how it handled personal data and allowed third-party apps access to users' information, including statements by senior executives such as CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

A jury on Sept. 25 sided with the state, finding 26 of 29 public statements by Facebook to be misleading and treating each as reaching large numbers of New Mexico Facebook users, producing a total of almost 43.9 million violations.

Under New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act, the maximum penalty is $5,000 per willful violation. Judge Francis J. Mathew of New Mexico's First Judicial District Court imposed the statutory maximum (roughly $219.5 billion) but reduced the award to $25 billion. Interest accrues at 15 percent annually until paid. Meta has said it will appeal.

"Facebook's wrongdoing - over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public - goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Mathew wrote in his order.

The jury's findings covered Facebook's statements on data practices, as well as its handling of hate speech, misinformation, and exceptions to platform rules.

"This is a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country," Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. "A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."

Meta did not immediately return a request for comment by The Epoch Times, but its chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, told Reuters the company is confident it will prevail on appeal.

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney said.

In the Cambridge Analytica scandal, the now-defunct British political consulting firm obtained personal information from as many as 87 million Facebook users and used the data for political profiling and targeted advertising. New Mexico alleged that Facebook misled users about third-party access to their data and the degree of control users actually had, and that after the Cambridge Analytica event the company's statements about investigations, audits, bans, and user notifications were also misleading.

This is Meta's second major courtroom loss in New Mexico this year.

In a separate case involving the safety of young users, a jury in March imposed $375 million in civil penalties on the company. On Aug. 6, a judge ordered Meta to pay an additional $567 million into a fund for youth mental-health remedies and imposed court-supervised changes to Facebook and Instagram, bringing the total financial exposure in that case to $942 million.

title: "Lost Its Mojo": Wolfe Downgrades Netflix As Billions In Content Spending Fails To Deliver Hits
desc:
"Lost Its Mojo": Wolfe Downgrades Netflix As Billions In Content Spending Fails To Deliver Hits

Wolfe Research downgraded Netflix early Thursday, warning that "bears are winning the engagement debate" and that the subscription-based streaming service "has lost its mojo."

"Engagement failed to respond to rising investment, and last week's content leadership changes convince us that solutions require patience & lower incremental margins. Attention economy competition is rampant. Consensus estimates look fair," analyst Peter Supino wrote in a note on Thursday morning.

Supino estimates that engagement in the US and Canada was flat to down in the first half of 2026, even as programming investment increased. YouTube continues to gain television viewing share, while competitors including Amazon, Apple, Disney and HBO are increasing spending.

"Despite $3B of content expense growth over the last 2 years, Netflix has lost its mojo. YouTube keeps gaining TV share," the analyst wrote.

The lack of major new hits is a key driver of Netflix's stalled subscriber growth. Aside from the final season of Stranger Things, Supino said the streaming platform has struggled to sustain viewership growth for its biggest shows and films.

Last week, chief content officer Bela Bajaria was abruptly booted and will be replaced later this month by veteran entertainment executive Peter Rice in hopes of delivering content that subscribers actually want to watch.

Netflix has transformed into a woke programming operation for kids...

Back to Supino: he noted that Netflix's valuation of about 17.5 times projected 2027 earnings makes shares look relatively inexpensive for a streaming platform expected to deliver double-digit revenue growth. However, he sees limited upside at this point unless Netflix can deliver global hits.

He also lowered his 2027 revenue forecast to $56.27 billion from $56.68 billion, implying 10.1% growth. He lowered his earnings estimate to $3.67 a share from $3.73.

title: Jobless Claims Near 60-Year Lows Amid 'Low-Hire, Low Fire, Low-Inspire' Economy
desc:
Jobless Claims Near 60-Year Lows Amid 'Low-Hire, Low Fire, Low-Inspire' Economy

The number of American filing for unemployment benefits for the first time dropped (again) last week to 194k - basically in line with 60 year lows...

Michigan saw the largest rise in initial claims last week while Ohio and Tennessee saw the biggest decline...

Continuing Claims ticked up but remains very close to 3 year lows...

The cleanest way to reconcile it is that this is a "low-fire, low-hire” labor market, with employers hoarding labor, not shedding it.

Of course, claims remain a poor gauge of how hard it is to get hired, since new entrants, re-entrants, and gig workers mostly can’t file.

Low firing plus low hiring means insiders feel secure while anyone outside the job market is stuck.

Of course, sentiment remains disastrously low, but we'd argue it’s mostly a prices story wearing a jobs costume (impacted by political bias within the polling).

The bottom line is that claims tell you a recession isn’t imminent, payrolls tell you momentum is fading, and sentiment tells you the median household is getting squeezed by prices rather than layoffs.

The risk is that this equilibrium breaks non-linearly: low-hire markets can flip to firing quickly once margins compress, and claims would be the last of the three to flag it, not the first.

title: Music Publishers Sue Anthropic For Copyright Infringement
desc:
Music Publishers Sue Anthropic For Copyright Infringement

Authored by Stacy Robinson via The Epoch Times,

A federal district court in California is set to hear arguments this week as a group of music publishers sues Anthropic, alleging that the artificial intelligence (AI) firm is stealing their work.

Led by Concord Music Group, the plaintiffs say that Anthropic trained its AI model, Claude, using copyrighted lyrics from their artists. The next hearing is slated for Oct. 21.

In a separate case, Concord alleges that Anthropic used pirated copies of 20,517 music works - accessed from torrent sites - to train Claude.

The lawsuits are just two of dozens of legal actions taken by publishers in the book, news, and art industries, as creatives argue that AI companies have trained their models on existing work with an intent to replace human ingenuity with machine outputs.

When prompted, Claude will create a new set of song lyrics that are similar to existing work, Concord says, or generate a new song using similar chord progressions.

"For example, when asked by Publishers' investigator to write "a song about the death of Buddy Holly," Claude generated a verbatim copy of the lyrics to 'American Pie,'" a court filing says.

The Claude AI tool will also spit out lyrics to copyrighted songs upon request, and Concord argues that this cuts into its profits.

If a web user wants to know the words to "Uptown Funk" or "Hey Jude," a simple Google search will bring up any number of websites containing the lyrics. But those websites pay a licensing fee to republish the lyrics. Getting the song texts for free through AI makes those websites obsolete, Concord argues, and deprives the publishers of that extra revenue.

For its part, Anthropic is arguing that the Fair Use doctrine allows it to use the song lyrics. That legal principle allows use of copyrighted work under certain circumstances, such as teaching or criticism, or when the copyrighted material is substantially transformed into something new.

Anthropic recently had to settle a case for $1.5 billion after a group of book publishers sued. It used the same fair use argument, but only with partial success.

Although the judge in that case agreed that using copyrighted material to train AI models was fair use, the company had initially used pirated versions of the books taken from the internet. That may end up being relevant for Concord's second lawsuit.

Anthropic also said that Claude contains "copyright-protective" features and that it isn't the company's fault when a user finds a workaround.

"When a system 'creates the copy only in response to the user's command,' its operator does not engage in volitional conduct," Anthropic said in a court filing. "The user does."

Concord is asking the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California in San Jose to award up to $150,000 per copyright violation, along with another $25,000 for instances where it alleges that Claude removed copyright notices from song lyrics. Or else, it at least wants the profits it lost by the infringement - an undisclosed amount Concord said it will later document in court.

At the end of last month, the plaintiffs submitted a short brief noting a recent appeals court decision they hope will galvanize their cases.

On Sep. 30, the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled against the fair use argument in a similar case where Thomson Reuters sued AI company ROSS Intelligence.

Reuters developed a legal research database called Westlaw, and the entries contain "headnotes," which are short, hand-crafted annotations that summarize the information. According to a court filing, ROSS hired an outside company to provide material to train its AI tool, and that company used 25,000 Westlaw headnotes for that purpose.

In ruling for Reuters, the Third Circuit said that this was not fair use, partly because the ROSS tool was specifically created to be a competitor to Westlaw.

However, California is covered by the Ninth Circuit, so the court won't be strictly bound by that precedent when it considers the Anthropic lawsuit.

French government bonds sold off earlier today, pushing 10-year yields above 5% as budget concerns and social unrest sent the country's borrowing premium over Germany to its highest since 2011.

The French 10-year yield climbed to 5.11%, its highest since 2002, while the spread over equivalent German debt widened to 174 basis points, according to Bloomberg data.

Separately, across the Atlantic, the 10-year US Treasury yield declined to 5.07% as EU equities weakened and US stock futures fell on concerns about an AI bubble.

UBS macro strategist Simon Penn wrote in a note to clients that the surge in French yields and the widening spread were due to "budget rejections."

Penn added more color:

The French 10-year yield has opened Thursday higher, at 5.05%, up 3.6bp on the day so far. That's pushed the spread to Germany out another 5.5bp.

The news flow has moved away from street protests and back to the roots of the budget. The government isn't finding any takers for its budget proposals so far. Though full formal votes on the entirety of the budget are still to take place, this week has already seen MPs reject reduced spending measures.

News that the rejections mean some EUR10 bn of deficit reductions have already been cast to one side, and the most contentious budget matters are still to be discussed has raised further the prospect of budget failure.

A week ago the working assumption in the markets had been that MP's would vent their frustrations with budget measures but stop short of outright rejection. That is not proving to be the case. The bond market is hence reacting accordingly. The next threat comes later Thursday afternoon if MPs indicate today's proposals to cut spending are also to be rejected.

In a separate update, Penn said:

The biggest argument in the French parliament on Thursday is likely to be on the government's proposal to limit pension indexation. Under the current plan, only around one-third of pensioners, primarily those on lower incomes, would continue to receive full inflation-linked increases, with larger pensions facing partial indexation or a freeze. The proposal is one of the largest sources of planned savings and has already encountered significant resistance during the committee stage. In fact, adjusted for shifts in utilization rates, total factor productivity growth was zero in Q2. Said otherwise, there has been zero productivity boost from AI!

And just in case anyone thought that was a throwaway line:

"Any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble. These bubbles, if we want to use that word, often coincide with these giant technological transformations."

In other words, the best-paid man in the room thinks the room is in a bubble, and he is fine saying so out loud. Which, for regular readers, will sound familiar: we have been warning since last October that the AI boom runs on debt, and lately the market has started doing the warning for us.

To be sure, nobody will care this is a bubble... until the market crashes, at which point everyone will scream how nobody warned them in advance. And just like that the new TBTF is born.

"Looking At Their Bills"

Griffin's timing was impeccable, maybe a little too impeccable. Hours earlier, the WSJ reviewed a fresh draft of Anthropic's S-1, which we broke down in "Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning." The short version: Anthropic booked $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, posted an $80.7 billion GAAP net loss (about $72 billion of which is a non-cash revaluation of financing instruments, leaving a still-hefty ~$8.7 billion underlying loss), and has signed more than $600 billion of mostly noncancelable compute contracts, with talks under way for another $150 billion. That would take the tab to as much as $750 billion.

Our reaction to the revenue headline was, well, brief:

*ANTHROPIC HAD $16.3B IN REVENUE IN FIRST HALF OF 2026: WSJ that's it?

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

Here is what that looks like on one chart: eventually someone has to pay for the blue bars, and Griffin just told us the customers are starting to check the invoices.

Griffin, for his part, said Anthropic's success will ultimately depend on proving to investors that its models are a must-have across every industry. That is a tall order when the price of the product keeps falling (and that ignores the fact that as "every industry" finds models are indispensably, it fires "almost every" worker currently employed, leading to a labor depression) . As we showed last week, Anthropic's token prices have tumbled to an all-time low:

Falling prices and decelerating growth are a tricky combination for a company with fixed, ten-year take-or-pay obligations. It is also why IPO investors marked the valuation down to $1.5 trillion last week after Anthropic's Q3 numbers showed the sequential growth rate hitting the brakes. Put differently, the bill keeps rising and the price per unit keeps falling, and the gap is what the IPO is supposed to fund.

From "Garbage" To "Depressed" To "Golden Era"

To be fair to Griffin, his AI views have had quite a year. Speaking in Davos in January, he called AI garbage, per Bloomberg. By May he told an audience at Stanford Business School that he was depressed by everything AI could achieve. On Tuesday he struck a sunnier tone, arguing the technology will unleash a wave of new business formation in the US:

"You're seeing the threat to white collar jobs playing out; as a business owner, you're seeing your competitive moats be filled in by bulldozers. At the same time, you're thinking that this will be a golden era for entrepreneurs."

Garbage, then depressing, then a golden era that happens to be a bubble. Three views in ten months is roughly how the market has traded AI too, so maybe he is just being consistent.

Griffin also pointed back to the days before the dot-com crash and some of the "fanciful" business models of that era:

"The companies that are on the other side of that bubble are the market leaders for decades to come. I just wish I'd kept my Amazon stock in that moment."

A fair point, with one footnote: anyone who kept their Amazon stock through that moment first had to sit through a drawdown of more than 90%. The winners on the other side of a bubble tend to get there the hard way.

Goldman: Breadth Is At Its Narrowest Since The Dot-Com Bubble

Griffin isn't the only one reaching for the 2000 analogy. Goldman's chief US equity strategist Ben Snider, in his latest US Weekly Kickstart (available to pro subs), notes that with the S&P 500 just 2% from its record high but the median S&P 500 stock 15% from its high, Goldman's preferred measure of breadth "remains near its narrowest level since the Dot-Com Bubble."

Snider also tackles the "productivity" question Griffin raised, from the earnings side. He expects S&P 500 EPS growth to slow from 29% in 2026 to 18% in 2027 (adjusting for accounting distortions), and warns that "slowing AI investment growth will be a fading tailwind." How big a tailwind? Goldman's Asia sales desk (Dani Wojdyla) puts it bluntly in this week's "Positioning Reset" note: "AI capex is currently contributing about half of S&P 500 EPS growth," an impulse Goldman expects "to diminish as capex growth slows and depreciation builds."

Translation: half of the earnings growth the market is paying for comes from companies spending money on AI, which shows up as someone else's revenue... and eventually as everyone's depreciation. The early Q3 read already shows the slope turning: 53% of S&P firms have beaten consensus EPS so far, above the 25-year average of 50% but well below the 64% rate of the past four quarters.

Last week Goldman's Tony Pasquariello argued breadth "isn't so bad"... then brought up the dot-com bubble twice, including a 2027 supply wildcard that could lift net US equity supply by the most since 2000. Anthropic's IPO, of course, is a big chunk of that wildcard.

Over at BofA, Michael Hartnett's team has done the bubble math on concentration. Peak concentration in the major bubbles of the past two centuries clustered around 40% (railroads were the outlier at 63%). The "AI Big 10" (Mag 7 plus Broadcom, AMD and Micron) recently hit 42%, above the 41% TMT peak in 2000:

Nothing says "healthy market" like a chart where the current reading sits between the Nifty Fifty and Japan in 1989.

Credit Got There First

If equity investors are only now discovering the word "bubble", the credit market has been pricing it for weeks. Per Goldman credit strategist Amanda Lynam's Global Credit Trader, "AI, Credit, and a Higher Cost of Capital" (also available to pro subs), USD HY AI-related spreads widened 25bp to 360bp over Treasuries, compared with just 2bp for non-AI issuers, with data center issuers leading the way:

Even Goldman's strategists, who just moved tactically overweight equities in their latest GOAL Kickstart, concede the point in the same note:

"Concerns on AI capex returns and funding are increasingly showing up in credit: CCC-BB spreads, hyperscaler CDS and neocloud OAS have all widened, with the latest move particularly sharp for neocloud issuers."

So Goldman is long the stocks and short the credit, while the credit is the one sending the warning. Their own Risk Appetite Indicator just "turned negative for the first time since March 2026," with all five sub-components down over the past month. Bullish, maybe... but not exactly confident.

The equity-credit gap is stark. As Goldman's basket desk showed in a chart we highlighted in "Trick Or Treat", hyperscaler equities were about 15% lower the last time hyperscaler credit spreads were this wide:

And the debt pile is only getting bigger. Goldman's credit team expects project finance plus direct hyperscaler issuance to hit $720 billion in 2027, up from $37 billion of project finance in all of 2025, with risks "firmly skewed to the upside":

The cracks are already showing where capital meets reality. Korea's Elice cratered 32% on its debut despite a retail tranche 400 times oversubscribed, and Australia's Nextdc imploded 45% and is mulling force majeure as protesters stall power to its Melbourne campus. Here is the updated casualty list:

Fink: The Bubble Can't Stop Inflating

Not everyone in the C-suite agrees with Griffin, or rather they agree, they just don't see any way out. Less than a day after the Citadel CEO's comments, BlackRock's Larry Fink took the opposite side, warning on Bloomberg TV from the Berlin Global Dialogue that the real danger is building too slowly. Per Bloomberg:

"If we don't build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost of compute is so high right now. And the faster we can build out more data centers, the more compute we have, the faster we can bring down the cost."

Incidentally, this is precisely the point we made a month ago:

The more data centers are lit, the faster this bubble pops

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) September 25, 2026

And, just to raise the stakes, Fink added that "If we slow down the build out of this technology, I think it really does jeopardize the economy." (Deutsche Bank's Christian Sewing, for what it's worth, also played down Griffin's bubble fears on Wednesday.)

Translation: the bubble is too important to stop inflating. Coming from the head of a firm whose infrastructure arm is among the biggest data center buyers on the planet, maybe that is not a huge surprise.

Fink does have a point on the physical bottleneck, and it is one we have been hammering for months: the constraint is power, permits and angry neighbors, which is why we keep arguing that "behind the meter" generation should be mandatory for new campuses. Nextdc's Melbourne fiasco is exactly that constraint in action, and so are the billions in Nvidia chips collecting dust in Amazon warehouses because there is nowhere to plug them in.

But the rest of his argument runs into the numbers above. If compute is so scarce and expensive, it is odd that Anthropic's token prices just hit an all-time low and its revenue growth is slowing (thank Chinese open-source models, which Dario is desperate to ban at the sovereign level). More importantly, building faster means borrowing faster, and Fink himself flagged the problem in the same interview:

"We're at a time now where we're finally unlocking private capital, and so the competition for capital is as large as I've ever seen in my professional career."

He also said bond yields are "flashing," adding: "Wake up, federal government. Our deficits are starting to have real large issues." Put the two together and you get the trade-off we have been describing for months: every extra dollar of AI debt is competing with Uncle Sam's ~$2 trillion deficit for the same duration buyers, with the 10Y already above 5%. As we noted on Sept 1, AI issuance has been crowding out Treasuries. In other words, Fink's cure for compute inflation (build more, faster, with borrowed money) is a fine recipe for bond-market inflation.

Who Holds The Bag On The Other Side?

Griffin's bubble call comes with a familiar bullish escape hatch: bubbles fund revolutions, and the survivors become the Amazons of the next two decades. That is probably right about the technology. It says very little about the price anyone pays to get there, or about who ends up holding the paper when the bills come due.

Griffin says it's a bubble; Fink says stopping it would be inflationary. Both can be right, which is precisely the problem. And right now the bills are piling up on both sides. On one side, Anthropic needs public investors to backstop as much as $750 billion of compute it has already promised to pay for. On the other, its biggest customers (per Griffin) are starting to ask what they are getting for their money. Meanwhile half of S&P earnings growth depends on the capex continuing, the credit market is already charging more to fund it, and the bond market (per Fink himself) is "flashing."

So we'll side with Griffin's first word over his last one. The AI buildout will probably produce a few generational winners, but the path from here to there looks a lot more like 2000-2002 than like a "golden era", and as usual, credit is telling equities which way the bubble deflates. If the man with the best seat in the house wishes he had kept his Amazon shares, maybe the more useful lesson is that he didn't buy more of them in March 2000.

desc:
EU Better Hope Global Warming Is Real As NatGas Withdrawals Begin With Dangerously Low Reserves

European natural gas futures climbed for a second day as countries began drawing on stockpiles already at exceptionally low seasonal levels.

Brussels is now left hoping that Greta Thunberg's global warming narrative is real to ease pressure on the region's fragile energy balance. Even then, one or two severe cold snaps could accelerate inventory depletion, intensify competition for LNG cargoes and push the energy-stricken continent toward another winter crisis, particularly if disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz continue to constrain LNG supplies.

Gas Infrastructure Europe data showed that EU NatGas inventories declined for the first time this year.

Storage sites are about 74% full, well below the 15-year average for this time of year and, according to Bloomberg data, at the lowest seasonal level in records dating to 2009. Germany's gas storage sites are just 61% full.

Dutch front-month futures, Europe's benchmark, breached 90 euros a megawatt-hour around 9:42 London time. Prices reached their highest since late 2022 earlier this week (read report) and have nearly tripled compared with last winter, increasing pressure on industry, freight and, of course, households.

The smaller buffer leaves Europe increasingly dependent on the international market, where it must compete with Asian buyers. This suggests TTF prices will have to rise sharply as the Hormuz maritime chokepoint remains chaotic.

Mild October weather across the bloc has eased heating demand and allowed utilities to stockpile additional reserves. The latest forecasts show warmer conditions returning to northwest Europe next week, though temperatures will fall next month, offering a warning of what lies ahead as the Northern Hemisphere enters the winter period.

Perhaps Europe will experience a slightly warmer-than-average winter because of strong El Niño conditions. But now is when elites in Brussels, who endlessly pushed the global warming narrative for years, must hope they are right. If they are not, all it could take is several cold snaps this winter to deplete inventories across the bloc to dangerously low levels, leaving less cushion to absorb shocks.

title: "Everyone Has Blown Up": London Macro Traders Carried-Out As French Carry Trade Implodes (Again)
desc:
"Everyone Has Blown Up": London Macro Traders Carried-Out As French Carry Trade Implodes (Again)

For the better part of three years, the hottest seat in London's multi-manager world was a European rates book: lever up French OATs in repo, clip the carry, collect the seven-figure payout. This month, the French bond market sent the bill.

According to a must-read report from eFinancialCareers' Sarah Butcher, London's macro hedge funds are quietly emptying out their EGB desks. Funds aren't talking about performance, but headhunters and bank traders who have been keeping score say the count of ejected European rates PMs and traders has climbed from the mid-70s a few weeks ago to close to 100 people. One senior trader at a liquidity provider summed it up in four words: "Everyone has blown up... they are all out"

In other words, the most crowded trade in European fixed income just found out what happens when the collateral is the problem.

And the bleeding hasn't stopped. This morning Bloomberg flashed that the French bond risk gauge is nearing 160bps, a fresh 15-year high, while French 10Y yields hit 5% for the first time since July 2002.

Below we walk through what blew up, why it blew up (twice), what Goldman, Morgan Stanley and the rest of the Street make of it, and why the market's attention is already drifting to the next domino: Italy.

The Trade: Borrow Against France, Pocket The Difference

The mechanics were simple enough to fit on a Post-it. Funds bought French government bonds, financed them in the repo market using those same OATs as collateral, and pocketed the gap between the bond's yield and the repo cost. Lever it up enough times and a few basis points of carry becomes a career. Per eFC, as French yields rose amid political chaos, OATs sold off and the whole highly leveraged structure was turned upside down.

A bank trader watching from the sidelines was less charitable:

"These people weren't even real portfolio managers," claims one senior trader, watching from the sidelines in a London bank.

"They were just using EGBs as a carry asset. Buying bonds, sitting on the carry and getting a percentage cut. It was fun for a while. You had a lot of PMs who were long France and long Italy, but with inflation coming in and rates high, it wasn't going to last."

Another PM in the sector offered a more philosophical take: "every bubble gets its moment."

The wider version of the trade, as Bloomberg reported on Oct 2, was the OAT asset-swap: funds including Taula Capital and Balyasny had built positions to harvest the spread between French yields and interest-rate swaps. Those were lucrative right up until the budget blowup of Oct 1, when the trades flipped from winners to liabilities and everyone hit the exit at once. RBC BlueBay's Kaspar Hense told Bloomberg what that looked like from the inside:

"Most typical hedge-fund strategies are in risk reduction mode. There have also been stop-loss levels triggered, partly on the steepener trades and now on long France trades." (emphasis ours)
— Kaspar Hense, RBC BlueBay Asset Management, via Bloomberg

Fidelity International's fixed income CIO Marion Le Morhedec went further, estimating that hedge fund activity could explain roughly half of the recent moves in the French-German spread, pointing to particularly heavy Eurex activity. Turns out the "liquidity providers" were also the liquidity takers.

Regular readers will recall that we called this one in real time on the very first day of the month:

it's been a while since we had a European sovereign debt crisis

*FRANCE-GERMANY 10-YEAR YIELD SPREAD WIDENS 8BPS TO 135BPS

France CDS widest in 13 years

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 1, 2026

...which was followed hours later by "Debt Crisis Back? European Bond Markets Crash, CDS Explode Amid France Budget Panic Contagion" (Oct 1). By the next day, the OAT-Bund spread hit 154bps, the widest since 2011, and the deleveraging was in full swing.

Same Trade, Same Crowd, Same Exit Door

The most damning detail in the eFC piece: according to the liquidity-provider trader, many of the PMs who blew up this month had already blown up in March, on the same positions. That was when the Iran war and the Hormuz shock triggered the first great European rates unwind, and when, per Bloomberg, multi-strats from Millennium to Balyasny to ExodusPoint gave back some or all of their year-to-date gains as crowded trades unwound.

Seven months apart, the same book got carried out twice. Diversification at its finest.

"They've blown up twice on the same trades."

Another trader observes that a lot of funds moved into the European fixed income space in the belief that it was easy money:

"The whole European carry system is now being questioned."

You can see both episodes in Goldman's own long-OAT/short-Bund rolling futures basket, which the bank's Systematic Trading Strategies desk circulated to clients: a steady grind higher for three years, a wobble in March, and then a near-vertical collapse that has wiped out roughly five years of gains as the basket fell from a February peak of ~104.3 to ~99.2.

Goldman's STS desk described the October contagion mechanism in that same note (available to pro subs here):

OATs have come roaring back into market focus over the last month. Where an unwind of popular rates positions following the latest ECB meeting (mostly steepeners), seemed to spread to wider carry trades in the rates space among a bid for volatility. A weak starting position for France with regards to debt and fiscal background and uncertainty into next year's election as well as challenging budget process didn't help. (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs STS, Tim Huiszoon, Oct 12

Translation: the steepener crowd got stopped out first, then the losses bled into every other levered carry position on the same risk books. Not a fundamental repricing so much as a margin call with a French accent.

Allianz Trade agrees, noting in an Oct 9 report that speculative shorts, hedge-fund asset-swap unwinds and thin liquidity created a negative loop, with market depth more than 50% below normal:

"The speed reflects a positioning shock, not a pure repricing of fundamentals. Long-term investors are sitting out ahead of the elections... Fragmentation is far from 2012 or 2020 levels, but the ingredients are in place." (emphasis ours)
— Allianz Trade, "Toasted, not burnt", Oct 9

Note the second sentence: the real money that would normally buy the dip is sitting on its hands until the election. Which leaves... nobody.

The Plumbing Problem Nobody Wanted To Talk About

It's not just about P&L. Hedge funds have stepped in as the marginal provider of liquidity in European sovereigns precisely as central banks, pensions and banks stepped back. Per Bank of France data cited by Reuters, French government debt accounts for roughly €100 billion of the €250 billion in euro-area sovereign bonds pledged as repo collateral. In other words, France is the euro repo market.

So far the repo market itself has held up, but the risk is obvious: a further ratings cut narrows the pool of institutions able (or willing) to take OATs as collateral, which raises funding costs, which forces more selling. Commerzbank flagged exactly this back in September after Fitch's downgrade:

"...once a second agency downgrades to single-A, OAT repos may cheapen visibly, similar to BTPs, where more than half of bonds already trade above the depo rate." (emphasis ours)
— Commerzbank, via MNI, Sep 16

With Moody's reviewing France on Friday, that is not exactly a theoretical concern. And as we noted when the sell-side spent a day insisting the OAT rout was "just positioning," the contagion had already jumped to the banks, with the selloff reactivating Europe's "doom loop" (Oct 7). Goldman's European financials desk is still hiding under the desk:

"We are staying in risk off mode on banks (topics remains Euro sovereign crisis fear + Rates + Competition + Agentic, ie peak ROTE)... Appetite for French banks is very low given how long it will take to have some clarity." (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs EU Financials specialist sales, Oct 20

"Overshot Fundamentals"... Says Goldman (Two Weeks Ago)

To be fair to Goldman, the bank has been leaning against the panic. Its strategists argued earlier this month that the OAT selloff appeared to have overshot fundamentals, amplified by positioning, though they conceded France is cheap relative to peers but lacks a catalyst. GS's STS desk went further on Oct 12, flagging GIR's expectation that the spread stabilizes at tighter levels and pitching a 1-year principal-protected option on OATs vs Bunds as a reversal trade with the 10Y spread at ~135bps.

The market had other plans. After weekend riots across France (nearly 2,400 arrests), the spread widened another 8bps to ~145bps on Monday, per Goldman's Daily Monitor, which ran this as its chart of the day: the OAT-Bund spread (inverted) dragging the euro down with it.

Goldman's FX desk confirmed the hedge funds were already heading for the exits:

"EUR option volumes – which have been an key indicator for broader portfolio hedges – have also decreased and are more than 30% off the highs. Certainly, a lot of hedges have been put on already and broad de-risking across popular positions was a hallmark of last week's activity." (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs FX desk, Oct 19

Bloomberg's Vassilis Karamanis reads the same options market more darkly: the premium for longer-dated euro downside now exceeds short-dated, suggesting the euro's weakness "reflects more than a positioning adjustment." So much for "just positioning."

By Monday's close, French 10Y yields had posted their highest close since 2002 (Oct 20), and on Tuesday the spread hit a 156bps peak:

French bonds getting smashed: OAT-Bund spread back to crisis wides.

Expect ECB monetization demands to return

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

And this morning the milestone everyone was waiting for finally printed: per Bloomberg, French 10Y yields hit 5% for the first time since July 2002, with the OAT-Bund spread out another 5bps to 158bps as Brent traded above $110. So much for stabilizing at tighter levels.

Goldman's own economists, meanwhile, aren't buying the government's numbers either. In Tuesday's European Daily, Alexandre Stott writes:

"Recent protests over school underfunding and cost-of-living pressures have been among the largest since the pension reform strikes of 2019 and 2023 and the 'yellow vests' movement of 2018... we remain sceptical that the government will meet its deficit target of 5.0% of GDP next year... Our poll-based model therefore continues to see Le Pen as the clear favourite to become President next year." (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs, European Daily: France—Budget Adoption Likely Later This Year, Oct 20

Morgan Stanley's chief global economist Seth Carpenter, whose note we published on Oct 11, is just as blunt about the arithmetic, and about the cavalry:

At wider than 150bps, the 30yr OAT-Bund spread surpassed the 130bp mark reached in the euro area debt crisis a decade ago... Debt stabilization would require a primary surplus of roughly 2% of GDP, a turnaround of about 5 percentage points. That shift would be larger than the adjustment required in Italy in the early 2010s... We think the bar for direct ECB intervention is very high, but France may not be the last test. (emphasis ours)
— Morgan Stanley, Seth Carpenter, Sunday Start

Put differently: the ECB is not coming to rescue anyone's carry book, and certainly not before Paris finds a fiscal squeeze bigger than the one Rome needed in 2011. Good luck with that during riots. Bill Blain, for his part, awarded a "No Sh*t Sherlock" prize to anyone who spotted European yields spiking after the riots, warning in Tuesday's Morning Porridge that the unrest could "metastasise into a potential bond crisis unless the ECB can swiftly demonstrate it is able, willing and stands ready to intervene."

Where Do 100 Ejected Rates Traders Go?

The career fallout is where the eFC report gets really fun. Some will drift back to the banks, where one headhunter said dealers need them to manage ECB exposure and bond books. The catch, per a bank trader: these PMs were pulling in $1 million-plus, a number that at a bank you only see as a desk head. Many are also tied up in non-competes, and some are still collecting guarantees and in no rush to find work. Good news for the departed PMs; allocators may see it differently.

Not everyone was pushed: one source estimated roughly 10% left voluntarily, some to raise their own funds, because allocators are struggling to find people both willing and able to take risk. Which is one way of describing a market where everyone who took risk just got carried out.

More ominous is the verdict from the trading floors: one trader told eFC that funds piled into European fixed income believing it was easy money, and that the whole European carry system is now being questioned. A bank trader called it systemic. And per the headhunter, the big fear now is that Italian BTP spreads go the way of OATs, a risk Morgan Stanley also flags, noting that wider OAT spreads are already putting pressure on BTPs.

Bottom Line

Goldman's bet is that this was a positioning flush: the levered carry crowd got shaken out, the forced selling is largely done, and spreads should drift back in. Maybe. But consider what has happened since the "overshoot" call: riots, a 5% 10Y, a spread nearing 160bps, a Moody's review on Friday, and a presidential race where Le Pen polls at 34%-38% in the first round. The forced sellers may be gone, but the natural buyers never came back, and the marginal bid in OATs for the past three years was a levered London pod that is now on gardening leave.

And this was never just about politics. Since the Hormuz crisis began, France has underperformed every major bond market, Italy included:

Which is why we lean toward the skeptics: this isn't the end of a positioning unwind, it's the beginning of a regime where France trades like the periphery, and where Italy, with the same crowd long it on the same leverage, is next in line. When the people who spent three years harvesting European carry are now warning that the asset class may never look the same, it's probably worth listening. Expect the ECB monetization chorus to get a lot louder. We'll check back after Friday's Moody's decision.

title: European Regimes Renew Their Attacks On Free Speech
desc:
European Regimes Renew Their Attacks On Free Speech

Authored by Ryan McMaken via Mises Institute,

In recent weeks, German and French politicians have denounced free speech, and especially the concept of "freedom of speech" as long envisioned in the libertarian tradition of natural rights. French President Emmanuel Macron on September 29 stated that"The so-called American 'free speech' today, which some people have promoted, is the opposite of free speech." Macron compared speaking freely as comparable to walking down the street assaulting other people.

A week earlier, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz declared,"Don't anyone come to me with free speech!" He asserted we must "still be able to protect citizens from false information."

Both were speaking on issues related to online speech through social media and similar platforms. Both see a grave danger to the ruling class posed by the ability of unvetted or anonymous users to post opinions freely.

In both cases, these attacks on freedom have been in the context of European regimes' repeated efforts to impose new regulations on social media platforms to limit speech.

This has been going on for several years. For example, back in February, Macron stated that "free speech is pure bullshit."

In Europe, the anonymity issue is no minor affair. In Germany, there are literal speech police who will arrest ordinary citizens merely for saying things online or reposting memes. It's easy to see why anonymity could be an essential tool in posting ideas and facts the regime doesn't like.

A European regime insisting on abolishing online anonymity is essentially tantamount to announcing that these regimes want the ability to make more arrests for wrongspeech. This is a growing problem across Europe, and a 2025 study concluded that British police were making 30 arrests per day for non-violent "offensive online messages." Under British law, one can be prosecuted for hurting someone else's feelings. That's not how British apologists describe it, of course, but that is the essential reality.

Euphemisms for Censorship

Whether we're talking about France, the UK, or Germany - all places where the despotic enemies of free expression have seemingly free rein - the regimes' forces do not, of course, come right out and say that they support censorship.

They couch their censorship in the soft language of Leftwing ideology. The claim is that speech must be regulated in order to combat "hate speech" or to reflect the "common good" or to combat "disinformation."

To wit, in recent years, European politicians have insisted that speech be made to fit into "a common framework" - to use Macron's phrasing - and to be subject to some standard determining what is "false information."

But here is the rub: Who is to determine what falls within this common framework? Who is to determine what constitutes "false information"? It is the ruling oligarchy and its political allies, of course, that will determine if some proposed fact or idea is to be allowed to be spoken freely.

The ruling elites will decide if some sentiment or phrase is to be defined as "hate speech" and thus will be punished by state police and regime jailers. The ruling elites will determine what is "science," and therefore what constitutes "disinformation." This was on full display in the United States during the Covid Panic, when the government bureaucrat Anthony Fauci effectively declared "I am the science."

It is through these state-created and reasonable-sounding "exceptions" to free speech that the regime smuggles in its despotism.

For example, this has been the case for many years with defamation laws. Those who defend legal sanctions for "defamation" essentially advocate for government censorship to combat hurt feelings. Moreover, for centuries, governments have used defamation laws as a means of punishing criticism of the regime. Laws against "seditious libel" - employed by absolutist kings of old - have always essentially been laws against free speech.

An Assault on Truth Itself

The individuals who are directly punished will not be the only victims of this censorship. Truth and critical thinking themselves will be the victims as the regime's subjects will no longer be allowed to fully and publicly examine the veracity of claims made by the ruling elites. It means that "truth" will be whatever the regime says it is.

This problem of using free speech to hide and distort reality itself was well described more than 100 years ago by the radical free-market libertarian Vilfredo Pareto. Pareto was no naive democrat who thought that freedom could necessarily be protected by elections or written constitutions. But he did understand that freedom of speech is at the very foundation of a free society, regardless of the type of regime or whatever other freedoms might be protected in writing.

Even as Pareto was facing the rise of violent radical socialists in Italy - and thoroughly doubted the ability of the liberal state to deal with it - he never wavered on the key importance of free speech. That is, Pareto remained a dogmatic hardliner on free speech, and in this was like nearly all libertarians before him, from the anarcho-capitalist Molinari to the American Revolutionaries.

Not surprisingly, then, Pareto concludes there were no "mitigating factors" that could legitimately limit speech in the name of some common good. Writing in 1916 he stated:

[B]efore a theory can be considered true, it is virtually indispensable that there be perfect freedom to impugn it. Any limitation, even indirect and however remote, imposed on anyone choosing to contradict it is enough to cast suspicion upon it. Hence freedom to express one's thought, even counter to the opinion of the majority or of all, even when it offends the sentiments of the few or of the many, even when it is generally reputed absurd or criminal, always proves favourable to the discovery of objective truth (accord of theory with fact). ...

Pareto goes on to insist that there can be no exceptions, even for the sake of protecting "truths" long held to be precious. Not even those assertions said to be essential to humanitarianism can be considered protected from the scrutiny of free speech. He continues:

Nor can an exception be made for humanitarian dogmas, nor for the dogmas of the sex religion so dear to Senator Berenger and other geniuses of the same magnitude. Let us keep the point strictly before us: There is no scientific liberty unless everything is open to doubt - even Euclid's geometry and three-dimensional space. It is ridiculous to say that one is disposed to grant liberty for "truth" but not liberty for "error"; for the point at issue is none other than to discover where the "truth" lies and where the "error"; and it cannot be settled if "error" cannot be defended by every possible reason that can be advanced in its favour. Only after such reasons have been validly refuted is judgment of error affirmed - pending further investigation. Many people fail to understand that, because in judging of truth or error they substitute a criterion of sentiment for the logico-experimental criterion.

Clearly, the fact that free speech is now so under siege in Europe is simply the latest evidence of how far out of favor old historical liberalism has become in Europe. Every year, Europe more enthusiastically embraces its worst tendencies in which human rights are repeatedly jettisoned to protect the "rights" of those who rule over the continent. Yet, the antipathy toward free speech also demonstrates the weakness of the European regimes and their political programs. Were the German, French, and British states not so hampered by political division, economic decline, and public dissatisfaction, they would not be so fearful.

Americans have no yet traveled so far down this road. But the foundation is already being built. Republicans support laws deeming all criticism of a certain foreign government to be "anti-semitism" and therefore "hate speech." Covid laid bare the American Left's enthusiasm for anti-speech tyranny. All that is necessary for the First Amendment to be wiped away is for a handful of federal judges to agree with the enemies of freedom. There is no guarantee.

title: Chancellor accepts Labour has put a ‘lot of pressure’ on business and says helping entrepreneurs will be a budget priority – UK politics live
desc:
John Healey is expected to cut red tape requirements, particularly for smaller businesses

Kalyeena Makortoff is the Guardian’s banking correspondent.

CS Venkatakrishnan, CEO at Barclays, seems to have admitted defeat over bank tax hikes, which are expected to be a headline measure in Healey’s budget next week.

I recognise that the chancellor and the government has been entrusted with an important duty by the public and the people. And they have to balance a host of considerations. He [Healey] is the man in the arena, and I deeply respect the responsibility he bears on his shoulders and wish him well.

His long term goal is the same as our long term goal, which is to get growth.

So what is the chancellor now concentrating on? One could be forgiven for thinking him utterly unreconstructed: a party man and proud of it. There is no such thing as Healeyism, he says when the conversation turns to Anthony Crosland’s evangelism for the mixed economy: “I’m just Labour.”

“Just Labour” is exactly what the bond markets fear — and, indeed, it is what gives Kemi Badenoch hope of pulling off a comeback to rank alongside Lazarus and Bobby Ewing for utter implausibility.

Healey argued that his budget next week would refute the claim made by Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, about Labour not having the right policies to promote growth. In an article for the Financial Times, Haldane said Conservative policies were better for the economy, partly because they were more likely to support “cuts to business and employment taxes and regulation to unleash animal spirits”. In his write-up, Maguire says:

It was Haldane who also said, memorably and mercilessly, that the markets had concluded that this was a “traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”. At Westminster, this sort of criticism is at risk of curdling into thick and immovable consensus. What does Healey say to that? “I’d say to Andy Haldane,” he growls, fixing me with a cold stare, “speak to me next Thursday.” And, for the record, he speaks explicitly of “making an argument for how you bring welfare costs down” — albeit not via the “crude cuts” that were Starmer’s undoing.

Healey hinted that he was sympathetic to arguments that Labour should drop its plan to let younger workers qualify for the full national living wage. In his article Maguire says:

[Healey] is “acutely conscious”, too, of the “trade off” between an ever-increasing minimum wage — particularly for the youngest workers — and levels of employment.

He knows the many businesses who “want to employ young people” sometimes cite that upward ratchet as a reason they cannot.

Healey defended the part he played in bringing down Keir Starmer. Healey resigned from Starmer’s government over defence spending, and this contributed to the loss of support for Starmer in the parliamentary party that led to him standing down. Referring to this period, Healey said:

The country was ready for a change … Wherever you stood on the spectrum of the [parliamentary Labour party], there was a recognition that we needed a change.

We have a very rare moment now. We’re in the middle of a parliament, the second half of a parliament, and we’ve got a chance of a new hearing. People are at least willing to listen again … the Labour party is actually quite determined and disciplined, and in any party, the second half of a parliament starts concentrating minds.

title: French Counterterror Police Arrest 'Ultra-Left' Activist Over Limoges City Hall Fire
desc:
French Counterterror Police Arrest 'Ultra-Left' Activist Over Limoges City Hall Fire

French police on Tuesday arrested a 34-year-old man suspected of taking part in the October 17 arson of Limoges city hall, three days after the riots that gutted the 1883 building. The elite RAID unit's Bordeaux branch took him at 6:15 a.m. in a small, isolated house at Val d'Issoire, in the Haute-Vienne department, according to the Limoges prosecutor's office. The prosecutor called him a "person suspected in the fire." He is presumed innocent and has not been charged.

A source close to the case told Franceinfo he is an "ultra-left activist" already on the "fiché S" security watchlist. Some outlets first reported his age as 40; Franceinfo corrected it to 34. The prosecutor said investigators identified him through "painstaking" cross-checking of images and videos. ICI, the public radio network, reports that he is from the neighboring Creuse department and is suspected of earlier sabotage of TGV overhead lines and construction sites. His record was clean until an appeal court convicted him of violence against a police officer at an October 2024 protest in Guéret, a ruling he has taken to the Court of Cassation, so it is not final.

The Justice Ministry says he was not alone. Spokesman Sacha Straub-Kahn told ICI that "we are certain, from the images, that this person did not act alone," calling it a "manifestly concerted action" and putting the crowd in front of city hall at 500 to 700 people with "fairly substantial pyrotechnic means." No accomplice has been named or arrested. The only source for the ultra-left label is an unnamed one, and neither the prosecutor nor the ministry has said what role the suspect is accused of playing.

Custody, which began Tuesday, can run to 96 hours because the case falls under the special regime for organized crime. The investigation is run jointly by Haute-Vienne police and the national counterterrorism sub-directorate (SDAT). The national anti-terrorist prosecutor's office has not taken the case, but is following it. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said Monday that anti-terror prosecutors would soon decide whether to treat the fire as a suspected terror attack.

The fire itself began around 6 p.m. Saturday, when masked protesters entered the town hall and set it alight, according to the prefecture. Prefect Maurice Barate said the fire was set deliberately. Overnight the roof and belfry collapsed, and only the modern rear section was saved. Nineteen people were taken into custody that day, and four police officers were seriously hurt. Prosecutors opened an inquiry into destruction of property by dangerous means by an organized group.

Mayor Guillaume Guérin says the state left his police to face the mob. Guérin, of the center-right Republicans, told Sud Radio that national police ran out of crowd-dispersal grenades at about 3:30 p.m. and fell back, and that he saw about 700 infiltrators among a march of roughly 5,000 (a figure the outlet did not verify). He told Public Sénat that 400 rioters faced only 30 municipal police officers, and that the state is "in part responsible" for what happened. He has asked for a special rebuilding plan like the one for Notre-Dame, full state funding of what insurance does not cover, and has said he may resign if he does not get it.

Reacting to the arrest, Guérin said he expects the courts to be "up to the task" and wants the suspect jailed, while noting the presumption of innocence, because "he destroyed the house of all Limousins." He has secured a riot-police company for next Saturday, saying he needs national police and CRS officers "to maintain order." Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to visit Limoges on Friday.

British landlords are being offered thousands more each month to house small-boat arrivals than local councils pay to shelter vulnerable British families, a Daily Mail investigation has revealed.

The deals come from Clearsprings Ready Homes, one of three Home Office contractors operating under multi-billion-pound taxpayer-funded contracts.

In one south London case, a landlord was offered £4,500 a month for a three-bedroom flat he currently rents to Southwark Council for £1,790. That is an extra £32,520 a year, plus bills, council tax and maintenance covered for three years.

The anonymous landlord told the Mail: "I already rent to Southwark Council, and they are able to offer significantly more than the local authority, which to me is bizarre. The council has a ceiling on what they are allowed to pay landlords like myself."

He continued, "For a three-bed flat I get £1,790 from the local authority to house families, while I would rent it to Clearsprings for £4,500 per month. I didn't go with them because it would have meant terminating my contract with Southwark Council and putting families at serious risk of homelessness. I am not prepared to do that. But many landlords just see it as an opportunity to earn more, and just go with them."

Here’s the kicker: The company, which has a taxpayer-funded contract worth around £7billion, is understood to be targeting landlords who currently provide accommodation to councils, students and vulnerable people, including those fleeing domestic abuse.

Clearsprings is understood to be targeting properties already used for council tenants, students and vulnerable people, including those fleeing domestic abuse.

The firm, run by Graham King (estimated fortune £726 million), houses around 30,000 asylum seekers and reported £62.6 million profit on £1.4 billion turnover in the year to January 2025.

A Home Office spokesman claimed that the department pays a capped contractual rate and that "any amount above that is covered by the contractor and not taxpayers."

Officials pointed to hotel closures and claimed savings of more than £1 billion on asylum support since the election, along with 80,000 removals.

Meanwhile, Border Security Commander Duncan Capps has warned that nearly 3,800 migrants are currently waiting in camps between Calais and Dunkirk - almost double the usual number of around 2,000.

Crossings so far this year are down on last year's total, but the backlog in northern France shows demand remains high. Migrants typically make multiple attempts; French intercepts do not lead to detention, so the same people can try again.

Since Labour took office in July 2024, more than 83,000 people have crossed in small boats - more than the roughly 83,000 personnel in the British Army.

Arrivals have at times averaged one every minute during peak periods. The system processing them has been described by a Home Office decision-maker who assessed thousands of claims as fundamentally broken.

Common patterns include package claims from the same nationalities using near-identical stories, staged photographs, and networks charging thousands of pounds to coach applicants to claim they are gay or face political persecution. Local residents have repeatedly protested when HMOs or former military sites are converted for this purpose.

The current Clearsprings offers simply accelerate the same displacement dynamic with higher guaranteed rents funded through the contractor model.

The pattern is consistent: record crossings, low removal rates, an asylum system described by its own officials as riddled with fraud, and now private contractors using the resulting demand to outbid councils for ordinary housing.

British families on the housing list, students, and people fleeing domestic abuse are being asked to compete against a taxpayer-backed premium for people who arrived illegally.

The contracts were set under previous governments; the volume and the political choice to keep the system running at this scale sit with the current one.

Without a sustained reduction in arrivals and a higher removal rate, the housing pressure and the cost will surely spiral out of control.

desc:
"Mobilization Will Be Massive": French Govt Plans To Send Soldiers To The Streets After Admitting Failures

French soldiers will take over guard duty so that police and gendarmes can be moved onto the streets for Saturday's expected protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told parliament on Tuesday.

Nuñez said troops from Operation Sentinelle, the anti-terror deployment, would replace internal security forces mainly on static guarding duties. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the same day that Saturday's mobilization of forces "will be massive," Remix News reported, ahead of a major protest planned for October 24.

— confrontation française (@confrontfr) October 17, 2026

Sentinelle was launched in January 2015 and keeps about 10,000 soldiers across France to guard against terrorist attacks, usually at places of worship, schools, tourist sites, railway stations and airports. It also covered the Paris 2024 Olympics and Paralympics. Nuñez described a post-holding role for the troops in this case, not a crowd-control one.

The government now admits it failed to contain last Saturday's riots. Lecornu acknowledged lapses in intelligence gathering, said police had been positioned too rigidly and said authorities chose not to cancel planned police leave, Reuters reported. He blamed far-left groups and framed the crisis as a choice "between violence and the Republic"; those groups say the government underestimated anger over living costs and declining public services. Nuñez told parliament: "I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility." He offered his resignation, and Macron rejected it.

About 60,000 police and gendarmes were on duty nationwide on Saturday, October 17, when roughly 500,000 people marched against the cost of living (authorities told Remix 550,000; organizers claimed over 800,000). Nuñez called that too few for the large crowds of rioters and looters on the edges of the marches. He said police had "lost control" in some cities and admitted a "lack of anticipation." Riots and looting hit Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities, and in Limoges an arson attack brought down the roof and tower of the historic town hall.

— Remix News & Views (@RMXnews) October 17, 2026

The toll so far is large. Euronews counts more than 2,500 arrests and Remix more than 2,400 detained, while Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin put the number in custody at over 2,330, 70% of them adults. Almost 1,000 members of the security forces were injured. Alain Di Crescenzo, president of the chamber of commerce, said more than 2,000 shops were hit and put the damage at "hundreds of millions of euros." On Monday Lecornu asked regional authorities for "localised and partial curfews" and said nearly 200 Paris police investigators would comb footage to identify looters. Parliament is also setting up a commission of inquiry into the causes of the unrest. As we reported, 8 p.m. curfews followed in northern cities.

Nuñez is also considering banning demonstrations that have not been declared and could lead to public disorder. Declared marches could be caught too, he said, but only if organizers or their stewards give authorities reason to think things will get out of hand. For marches judged low-risk, routes should steer clear of public buildings and high streets, and intelligence services are to step up estimates of turnout, especially of the most radical participants. He said security forces need more "responsiveness and mobility" against "scattered" and "extremely mobile" groups, and told parliament: "We will be there."

The playbook has a precedent. In March 2019, for the 19th Saturday of the yellow vest protests, Sentinelle troops guarded sensitive sites so police could focus on order, and demonstrations were banned on the Champs-Élysées and in central districts of Bordeaux, Toulouse, Marseille, Nice and Rouen. Police made 31 arrests and issued 15 fines for entering banned areas, out of 2,322 street checks in Paris, NBC News reported. Macron brushed off opposition criticism of the army's involvement: "Those trying to scare people, or to scare themselves, are wrong."

Ministers of that period drew a line at confrontation. Armed forces minister Florence Parly said it was "hors de question" to put soldiers face to face with protesters, and said Sentinelle would relieve police and gendarmes of counter-terrorism tasks. Nuñez's description of static duties fits that model, though the government has not said where in the country the troops will be posted.

The unrest is also reaching the bond market. We reported this week that French 10-year yields hit 24-year highs near 5%, with the spread over German Bunds close to 160 basis points and Moody's due to review France's Aa3 rating, which carries a negative outlook. title: NATO To Increase Black Sea Presence Following Drone Attacks On Shipping
desc:
NATO To Increase Black Sea Presence Following Drone Attacks On Shipping

Authored by Victoria Friedman via The Epoch Times,

NATO will send additional military equipment and aircraft to the Black Sea, following a series of drone attacks on shipping vessels in the key waterway.

Ships wait in the Black Sea in Constanta, Romania, on Oct. 15, 2026. Andreea Campeanu/Reuters

Allison Hart, NATO's principal spokeswoman, said in an Oct. 20 post on X that the assets will support surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensic activities.

The decision came after NATO ambassadors met at the North Atlantic Council, the defense alliance's main decision-making body, to discuss Black Sea security.

"We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe," Hart said.

NATO's military spokesman, U.S. Army Col. Martin L. O'Donnell, said that in addition to sending the radar systems, drones, and patrol aircraft, allies will send or have sent intelligence agents and teams to conduct forensic examinations of explosives used against shipping vessels.

NATO has not attributed the attacks to any country.

The added presence comes in response to several Black Sea incidents in which drones struck cargo vessels.

Earlier this month, a number of cargo ships were hit off the Bulgarian coast of the Black Sea in the space of one week.

On Oct. 13, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity was sunk, and the Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, registered in Odesa, and Ukrainian-owned, was also struck.

Drones struck two other cargo ships in the same waters on Oct. 6.

Bulgaria said that Russia was likely behind recent incidents off its waters. Russia's ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, said at the time that she had no information from the Russian Ministry of Defense about attacks on commercial vessels.

Tankers Struck Near Romanian Coast

On Oct. 15, drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them both ablaze.

The vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea. It is a major export route for Ukraine.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan called the situation in the waters "serious."

"Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured, and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria," Dan said. "Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake."

Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the European Affairs Department at the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told Russian newspaper Izvestia on Oct. 20 that against the backdrop of NATO's increased reconnaissance activities in the Black Sea, "the risk of incidents, including unintentional ones, is indeed increasing."

Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania, Russia, Turkey, and Ukraine border the Black Sea, and it is a vital shipping route.

Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine is also among the world's largest producers of grain and seed products - both use the Black Sea to export their goods. Consequently, the waterway has become a target for both sides in the ongoing war.

In recent months, Russian forces struck Ukrainian targets on the Black Sea, including the ports of Chornomorsk and Odesa.

Ukraine, for its part, has been targeting Russian grain and farming infrastructure in the waters.
